Threat.value: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Memory.value: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.

I have permanently changed for the worse
The world is a dangerous place

issues.explanation: Funerals/graves is hard to reconcile as a primary trigger for a life-threatening motor vehicle collision when the rest of the profile does not reference death-related loss, bereavement, or fatality cues; it stands apart from the other trigger and appraisal content in a way that is clinically difficult to explain.

Failed Role suggests a strong role-based or responsibility-based meaning of the trauma, but the rest of the profile does not indicate injury-related incapacity, inability to work, or family-protector themes that would support this appraisal. For this patient, it feels insufficiently grounded in the surrounding items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
issues.explanation: 'Permanent humiliation' is not impossible after a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, but in this profile it sits awkwardly with the rest of the formulation and item set, which otherwise centers on fear-based post-collision threat, sensory reliving, and vulnerability rather than shame/humiliation. It is the least clinically integrated appraisal here and is hard to explain without other supporting shame-related items.

'Entrapment: Having no options' is not a clear contradiction, but for this trauma/profile it is weakly integrated compared with the other trigger items. The rest of the profile emphasizes crash reminders, reliving, danger appraisals, and hyperarousal. A strong entrapment trigger would usually be better supported by appraisals or memory content about being trapped or unable to escape, which are absent here.

vignette: Emiliano's life was forever altered on that fateful evening when his car was T-boned by another vehicle at an intersection. He vividly recalls the screeching tires, shattered glass, and crunching metal - sounds that still echo in his mind like a haunting refrain. As he struggled to free himself from the wreckage, Emiliano's thoughts were consumed by fears of not being able to escape, of being trapped, and of succumbing to his injuries. Miraculously, he survived with only minor physical harm, but the psychological toll was far more devastating. In the weeks that followed, Emiliano found himself increasingly on edge whenever he ventured out into the world. The sound of shouting - whether it was a child's playful laughter or an argument between strangers - would send his heart racing and transport him back to that moment of impact. Even the sight of cars with dented fenders or shattered windshields would trigger an overwhelming sense of dread, as if he were reliving the accident all over again. Loud noises - whether it was a slammed door or a blaring car horn - made him jump, and the familiar hum of his school's corridors became an ominous reminder of potential dangers lurking around every corner. As the Principal of his school, Emiliano felt like he was losing control. The slightest delay in his daily routine would send his mind spiraling into catastrophic thinking: "Something bad is happening; something terrible has occurred." His sleep began to suffer as well, with nightmares about the accident and an inability to shake off the feeling of being constantly on high alert, even when lying safely in bed beside his wife. Simple tasks like grading papers or attending staff meetings became Herculean challenges, as if he was perpetually waiting for the other shoe to drop. Emiliano tried to cope with these symptoms by avoiding anything that might remind him of the accident - including going to work. He'd tell himself, "I'll just take one more day off; I'm not ready yet." But this only led to feelings of guilt and inadequacy, as if he was somehow failing his students and staff. When he did manage to drag himself to school, he found solace in forcing positive thoughts into his mind - a desperate attempt to crowd out the darkness with affirmations of safety and control. However, this mental juggling act often left him feeling drained and anxious. As time went on, Emiliano began to overeat as a way to manage his distress. He'd devour entire pizzas by himself or snack incessantly throughout the day, hoping that the fleeting comfort of food would quiet the constant din of anxiety in his mind. His wife grew concerned about his weight gain, but Emiliano couldn't seem to stop himself. Despite these maladaptive strategies, the memories of the accident continued to haunt him. He'd relive the crash in vivid detail - the sights, sounds, and smells - as if it were happening all over again. The recollections felt so real that he'd often find himself ducking or flinching, as if expecting another impact. These flashbacks left Emiliano shaken, feeling like he was permanently changed for the worse. As the days turned into weeks, and the weeks into months, Emiliano began to see the world through a lens of fear. He became convinced that the world was a treacherous place, full of hidden dangers waiting to pounce. This realization made him question his own competence - "Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation" - and fueled his self-doubt. One fateful evening, as Emiliano was driving home from school, he caught himself checking the rearview mirror for what felt like the hundredth time, convinced that another car was about to slam into him. It was then that he realized he needed help. He couldn't keep living in a state of constant hypervigilance, perpetually waiting for disaster to strike. With a heavy heart and a deep sense of trepidation, Emiliano made the decision to seek professional help - hoping against hope that someone could guide him out of this darkness and back into the light.
